Cell adhesion molecules are a broad class of cell-surface and junction-associated proteins that mediate cell-cell and cell-extracellular matrix interactions and thereby organize tissue architecture, mechanical coupling, barrier integrity, migration, and signal transduction. This pathway includes cadherins, integrins, selectins, junctional adhesion molecules, and members of the immunoglobulin superfamily such as intercellular adhesion molecule-1, vascular cell adhesion molecule-1, neural cell adhesion molecule-1, platelet endothelial cell adhesion molecule-1, and related receptors. These molecules do not function merely as structural tethers; rather, they transduce biochemical and mechanical signals that regulate survival, proliferation, differentiation, polarity, cytoskeletal organization, and inflammatory cell trafficking. Foundational reviews emphasize that integrins, cadherins, immunoglobulin superfamily adhesion molecules, and selectins are central mediators of tissue organization and signal modulation, linking extracellular matrix composition and cell contact to intracellular pathways that govern cell fate and function [[198]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/9647866). Additional work shows that adhesion molecules are dynamically regulated and can influence cell survival and differentiation programs, as illustrated by studies of human pluripotent stem cells in which E-cadherin, classic cadherins, integrins, and heparan sulfate proteoglycans shape survival and lineage commitment [[199]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22647941). In vascular and inflammatory settings, endothelial adhesion molecules such as vascular cell adhesion molecule-1, intercellular adhesion molecule-1, E-selectin, and junctional adhesion molecules control leukocyte adhesion, transmigration, endothelial permeability, and vascular remodeling, processes that are highly relevant to chronic cardiovascular disease [[200]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29614819) [[201]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35356274) [[202]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27111582).

Taken together, these observations provide a useful framework for considering how this pathway could be related to heart failure, even though the cited studies are not focused exclusively on that condition. Although the provided publications are not focused specifically on heart failure, they strongly support a mechanistic link between the cell adhesion molecules pathway and heart failure through three convergent processes: inflammatory leukocyte recruitment, endothelial activation and barrier dysfunction, and maladaptive tissue remodeling. Heart failure is increasingly recognized as a chronic inflammatory and vascular remodeling disorder in which activated endothelium expresses adhesion molecules that capture circulating leukocytes and promote their entry into the myocardium and vasculature. In this regard, vascular cell adhesion molecule-1 and intercellular adhesion molecule-1 are especially important because they mediate inflammation-associated vascular adhesion and transendothelial migration of monocytes, macrophages, and lymphocytes; this biology is directly relevant to the immune cell accumulation that drives myocardial injury, fibrosis, and progressive ventricular dysfunction in heart failure [[200]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29614819) [[203]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31231358) [[204]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/3109455). Experimental evidence that suppression of tumor necrosis factor alpha-induced vascular cell adhesion molecule-1, intercellular adhesion molecule-1, and E-selectin reduces monocyte adhesion to endothelial cells further supports the concept that adhesion molecule upregulation is a proximal determinant of vascular inflammation, a well-established contributor to heart failure progression [[205]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26861272). Junctional adhesion molecules add a complementary layer of relevance because they regulate endothelial permeability, leukocyte recruitment, cell migration, and vessel wall interactions; studies in fibrotic liver disease show that junctional adhesion molecule-B and junctional adhesion molecule-C increase during chronic injury and participate in endothelial-pericyte type interactions and contractile remodeling, illustrating how adhesion programs can stabilize abnormal vasculature while promoting tissue fibrosis and altered microvascular tone, features that parallel microvascular dysfunction and interstitial remodeling in failing hearts [[202]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27111582) [[201]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35356274). More broadly, reviews of adhesion receptor signaling establish that integrins, cadherins, and immunoglobulin superfamily molecules integrate extracellular matrix cues with cytoskeletal and survival pathways, thereby controlling tissue integrity and cellular responses to stress [[198]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/9647866). In the context of heart failure, these functions are highly pertinent because cardiomyocyte mechanical coupling, endothelial homeostasis, fibroblast activation, and inflammatory cell trafficking all depend on precisely regulated adhesion signaling; when dysregulated, the result is enhanced immune infiltration, extracellular matrix remodeling, fibrosis, and decline in cardiac performance. Thus, the cell adhesion molecules pathway appears plausibly and substantially related to heart failure pathogenesis, particularly through endothelial activation, chronic inflammation, and remodeling of the cardiac interstitium and microvasculature.[[198]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/9647866) [[199]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22647941) [[203]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31231358) [[204]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/3109455) [[200]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29614819) [[205]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26861272) [[202]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27111582) [[201]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35356274) 

This general mechanistic context is also consistent with the enrichment results observed in the present analysis. There were 28 heart failure-associated proteins significantly enriched in the pathway of cell adhesion molecules, a functionally broad and biologically central category of cell-surface and junction-associated proteins that coordinates cell-cell and cell-extracellular matrix interactions, tissue architecture, mechanical coupling, barrier integrity, migration, and signal transduction. This enrichment is highly relevant to heart failure because adhesion-dependent signaling regulates several processes that are quantitatively and mechanistically linked to cardiovascular remodeling, including inflammatory cell trafficking, endothelial permeability, cytoskeletal organization, survival signaling, and extracellular matrix communication. The pathway definition encompasses multiple major adhesion protein families, including cadherins, integrins, selectins, junctional adhesion molecules, and immunoglobulin superfamily members such as intercellular adhesion molecule-1, vascular cell adhesion molecule-1, neural cell adhesion molecule-1, and platelet endothelial cell adhesion molecule-1, indicating that the 28 enriched proteins likely span several complementary adhesion modules rather than a single molecular axis. Foundational evidence has established that these adhesion systems act not only as structural connectors but also as bidirectional signaling regulators that couple extracellular matrix composition and cell contact status to intracellular pathways controlling proliferation, differentiation, polarity, and survival [[198]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/9647866). Additional data further support the dynamic and regulatory nature of adhesion molecules, showing that classic cadherins, integrins, and related surface proteoglycan systems influence both survival and lineage commitment decisions in human pluripotent stem cells, thereby reinforcing the concept that adhesion pathways exert measurable control over cell fate programs rather than serving solely passive structural roles [[199]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22647941). In cardiovascular and vascular inflammatory contexts, endothelial adhesion molecules including vascular cell adhesion molecule-1, intercellular adhesion molecule-1, E-selectin, and junctional adhesion molecules have been shown to regulate leukocyte adhesion, transendothelial migration, endothelial permeability, and vascular remodeling, all of which are processes directly pertinent to chronic heart failure pathobiology and progression [[200]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29614819) [[201]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35356274) [[202]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27111582).

To further contextualize these 28 proteins, the interaction network is shown below for visual assessment of connectivity and functional relatedness. The protein-protein interaction network visualization of these 28 proteins is provided below, together with the link to the STRING webpage for interactive inspection of network connectivity and functional relationships.

![PPI Network](imgs/b585aaa3-0601-4965-85cf-2d65466c4221.png)
![Link to the STRING webpage](https://string-db.org/cgi/link?to=060AA90D082E0551)

With this network-level overview in place, the following paragraphs introduce several of the significant proteins identified in the enrichment analysis and discuss their possible relevance in a more focused manner. During the function enrichment analysis, we identified serveral significant proteins. We will introduce them in-details in the following.

Among the proteins listed, ITGAV stands out as one of the most relevant to heart failure because it lies at the intersection of extracellular matrix remodeling, angiogenesis, inflammatory signaling, and TGF-beta activation. These processes are central to the pathogenesis of heart failure, particularly in ventricular remodeling and fibrosis. The ability of alpha-V integrins to bind matrix proteins such as fibronectin, fibrinogen, laminin, osteopontin, and thrombospondin suggests a direct role in the dynamic remodeling of the cardiac interstitium that accompanies pressure overload, ischemic injury, and chronic myocardial stress. Most notably, ITGAV-containing integrins activate latent TGF-beta-1, a master profibrotic cytokine strongly implicated in fibroblast activation, extracellular matrix deposition, and myocardial stiffening. Because excessive TGF-beta signaling contributes to adverse remodeling and progression toward both systolic and diastolic heart failure, ITGAV is mechanistically linked to a major disease-driving pathway. Its additional roles in angiogenesis and wound healing further support relevance to post-injury cardiac repair, where dysregulated neovascularization and scar formation can influence long-term ventricular function.[[206]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/10025398) [[207]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/9827803) [[208]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25127859) [[209]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/11323698) [[210]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24935931) 

In a related but somewhat more endothelial-centered context, JAM2 may also be relevant to heart failure because endothelial activation and leukocyte recruitment are key features of cardiac inflammation, which in turn drives tissue injury, fibrosis, and progressive dysfunction. The documented role of JAM2 in leukocyte tethering, rolling, and transmigration indicates that it could influence inflammatory cell entry into the myocardium or vascular wall. In heart failure, especially after ischemic injury or during chronic inflammatory remodeling, excessive leukocyte infiltration can amplify cytokine production, matrix degradation, and fibroblast activation. JAM2 may therefore contribute to the inflammatory vascular interface that promotes adverse remodeling. Its suggested role in angiogenesis is also pertinent, as microvascular dysfunction and maladaptive vascular remodeling are increasingly recognized components of heart failure pathophysiology. Thus, JAM2 is notable as a molecule connecting endothelial barrier biology, inflammation, and vascular adaptation.[[211]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/11590146) [[212]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/11823489) [[213]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24357068) [[214]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12239159) [[215]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12070135) 

Consistent with this emphasis on transendothelial immune trafficking, CD99L2 is potentially important in heart failure because leukocyte extravasation is a fundamental step in inflammatory tissue injury and repair. By promoting leukocyte passage across the endothelial basement membrane, CD99L2 may facilitate accumulation of inflammatory cells within the myocardium. This is particularly relevant in settings such as myocardial infarction, myocarditis, and chronic heart failure, where persistent immune cell infiltration contributes to cardiomyocyte injury, extracellular matrix remodeling, and fibrotic progression. Although the provided annotation does not directly mention cardiac tissue, the specific role of CD99L2 in the terminal phase of transendothelial migration makes it mechanistically plausible as a regulator of cardiac inflammatory burden. Proteins controlling this step are often influential in determining the magnitude and duration of tissue inflammation, and therefore may affect progression toward adverse ventricular remodeling.

Shifting from immune cell entry to vascular adaptation, JAM3 is relevant to heart failure primarily through its vascular functions. Endothelial chemotaxis and angiogenesis are essential for adaptive tissue repair after ischemic or pressure-induced cardiac injury. In the failing heart, capillary rarefaction, endothelial dysfunction, and insufficient compensatory angiogenesis can worsen hypoxia, impair metabolic support to cardiomyocytes, and accelerate ventricular dysfunction. A protein that promotes endothelial migration and angiogenesis may therefore influence the balance between adaptive vascular repair and maladaptive remodeling. Although the annotation is concise, JAM3 stands out because vascular insufficiency is a major determinant of heart failure progression, especially in ischemic cardiomyopathy and in hypertrophied myocardium where capillary density may become inadequate.

A related dimension of remodeling involves the extracellular matrix itself, which brings attention to VCAN. VCAN is of substantial interest in heart failure because extracellular matrix remodeling is a defining feature of adverse cardiac remodeling. As a hyaluronan-binding matrix proteoglycan involved in cell-matrix interactions and regulation of cell motility and differentiation, versican is well positioned to influence fibroblast behavior, inflammatory cell retention, and tissue structural organization. In the diseased heart, expansion and compositional alteration of the extracellular matrix contribute to fibrosis, ventricular stiffening, and impaired electrical-mechanical coupling. Molecules such as VCAN may shape the provisional matrix that forms during injury and remodeling, thereby affecting both scar architecture and chronic interstitial fibrosis. Its role in intercellular signaling further suggests that VCAN could modulate communication among fibroblasts, immune cells, and vascular cells within the failing myocardium.

Another matrix-associated molecule that may be relevant in this setting is SDC1. SDC1 is potentially relevant to heart failure because it integrates cell-surface signaling with extracellular matrix interactions, both of which are central to myocardial remodeling. As a proteoglycan linking cells to the interstitial matrix, SDC1 may influence mechanotransduction, inflammatory signaling, and matrix organization in stressed cardiac tissue. Its role in exosome biogenesis is also noteworthy, since extracellular vesicle signaling is increasingly recognized as a contributor to intercellular communication in heart failure, including crosstalk among cardiomyocytes, fibroblasts, endothelial cells, and immune cells. Through these mechanisms, SDC1 could affect fibrotic signaling, vascular responses, and inflammatory remodeling. While the annotation does not explicitly mention cardiovascular biology, the combination of matrix interaction and vesicle regulation makes SDC1 a plausible modifier of heart failure progression.[[216]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/8163535) [[217]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/8898217) 

Extending this theme of extracellular vesicle biology, SDC4 merits attention in heart failure because exosome-mediated communication has emerged as an important mechanism in cardiac remodeling, inflammation, and fibrosis. By regulating exosome biogenesis, SDC4 may influence the release of signaling cargo such as microRNAs, cytokines, and matrix-modifying factors from cardiac and vascular cells. In the setting of heart failure, these extracellular vesicles can modulate fibroblast activation, endothelial behavior, and immune responses, thereby shaping disease progression. As a syndecan family member, SDC4 is also likely to participate more broadly in matrix-associated signaling and mechanosensitive responses, which are highly relevant in pressure-overloaded and remodeling myocardium. Even though the provided annotation is limited, its role in vesicle biology makes it a potentially meaningful contributor to intercellular signaling networks in heart failure.

In addition to matrix and vascular remodeling, immune effector regulation may represent another potentially relevant axis, which highlights NECTIN2. NECTIN2 is relevant to heart failure mainly through immune and inflammatory mechanisms. Cytotoxic lymphocyte activation is increasingly implicated in myocardial injury in conditions such as viral myocarditis, inflammatory cardiomyopathy, and chronic heart failure with persistent immune activation. A receptor that enhances NK-cell and cytotoxic T-cell responses could influence the extent of immune-mediated cardiomyocyte damage or the clearance of stressed and infected cells. The downstream activation of PI3K, PLCG1, ERK, AKT, and calcium signaling underscores that NECTIN2 is not merely adhesive but actively immunostimulatory. In a heart failure context, this may be a double-edged sword: beneficial for antiviral defense or tumor surveillance, but potentially detrimental if it sustains maladaptive cardiac inflammation. Therefore, NECTIN2 stands out as an immune checkpoint-like adhesion molecule with plausible relevance to inflammatory forms of heart failure.[[218]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/8673704) [[219]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/9712030) [[220]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26755705) [[221]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31253644) [[222]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30591568) 

Finally, a further immune-related molecule of possible interest is SIGLEC1. SIGLEC1 may have an indirect but potentially meaningful connection to heart failure through viral and immune-mediated mechanisms. Viral infections are well-established causes of myocarditis, which can progress to dilated cardiomyopathy and chronic heart failure. By facilitating viral entry into activated dendritic cells, SIGLEC1 may modulate viral dissemination, antigen presentation, and downstream immune activation. These processes can influence both antiviral defense and immunopathology. In settings where viral myocarditis contributes to long-term ventricular dysfunction, molecules involved in host-virus interactions are biologically relevant. Although the annotation does not specifically address cardiac disease, SIGLEC1 stands out because viral-triggered inflammation is an important etiologic pathway leading to heart failure in a subset of patients.

### Neutrophil degranulation (REAC:R-HSA-6798695) 

Neutrophil degranulation is a core effector process of innate immunity in which activated neutrophils mobilize and release the contents of intracellular granules into phagosomes or into the extracellular space. These granules contain proteases, oxidant-generating enzymes, antimicrobial peptides, matrix-degrading enzymes, and inflammatory mediators that are normally used to eliminate pathogens and clear damaged tissue. Granule subsets are released in a regulated sequence and include secretory vesicles as well as tertiary, secondary, and primary granules, each carrying distinct cargoes such as matrix metallopeptidase nine, lactoferrin, myeloperoxidase, neutrophil elastase, defensins, azurocidin, and related inflammatory proteins. Although this process is essential for host defense, excessive or misdirected extracellular degranulation can injure host tissue by promoting oxidative stress, endothelial activation, extracellular matrix degradation, vascular leakage, thrombosis, and amplification of leukocyte recruitment. The pathway is particularly relevant in ischemic and inflamed tissues, where hypoxia can further enhance release of destructive granule contents. In cardiovascular settings, neutrophil degranulation is rapidly triggered after myocardial infarction and ischemia reperfusion, where it may contribute both to clearance of necrotic material and to collateral injury, ventricular wall thinning, adverse remodeling, and impaired recovery of cardiac function. Thus, neutrophil degranulation may be understood as a double-edged inflammatory pathway whose magnitude, timing, and molecular composition could influence whether it supports repair or instead promotes progression toward structural and functional cardiac failure.

Building on this biological framework, the available literature supports a mechanistic link between neutrophil degranulation and heart failure by showing that this pathway is activated in cardiac injury states that commonly precede or aggravate heart failure, and that its molecular products may directly promote the forms of inflammation, matrix remodeling, microvascular dysfunction, and contractile impairment that underlie adverse cardiac remodeling. A focused review on myocardial infarction concluded that neutrophil infiltration and degranulation occur immediately after infarction and shape both injury and repair, with released granule proteins such as myeloperoxidase, neutrophil elastase, neutrophil gelatinase associated lipocalin, matrix metallopeptidase eight, matrix metallopeptidase nine, cathelicidin, arginase, and azurocidin influencing infarct severity and prognosis; these processes are highly relevant because post infarction remodeling is a major route to heart failure [[223]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35410418). Experimental evidence further shows that macrophage derived signals regulate the intensity of neutrophil degranulation after myocardial infarction: murinoglobulin one restrains, whereas galectin three amplifies, matrix metallopeptidase nine release, and the balance between these mediators correlates with infarct wall thickness, suggesting that excessive degranulation may contribute to infarct wall thinning, a structural change strongly linked to later ventricular dysfunction and heart failure [[224]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35230372). In myocardial ischemia reperfusion injury, platelet derived serotonin was shown to intensify neutrophil degranulation, increasing myeloperoxidase release, hydrogen peroxide production, leukocyte adhesion, infarct inflammation, and loss of myocardial salvage, while depletion of platelet serotonin reduced degranulation and preserved cardiac function, thereby directly connecting this pathway to functional deterioration of the heart [[225]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30586717). Beyond infarction, clinical evidence in type two diabetes mellitus found that biomarkers of neutrophil degranulation characterize a restrictive echocardiographic pattern with diastolic dysfunction, supporting the possibility that chronic low grade activation of this pathway is associated with myocardial stiffening and an early heart failure phenotype even outside acute coronary injury [[226]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34129696). Related cardiovascular evidence from atrial fibrillation demonstrated that neutrophil degranulation is a pivotal over represented process in diseased atrial tissue and is extensively shared with pathways involving metabolism, cellular disassembly, and ion homeostasis, suggesting that degranulation may integrate inflammatory and structural remodeling programs that also favor progression to heart failure in arrhythmia associated heart disease [[227]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33536523). More broadly, studies in hypoxic and inflammatory conditions show that low oxygen tension enhances neutrophil granule exocytosis and release of destructive proteins, a finding that appears highly pertinent to the failing heart because myocardial ischemia, venous congestion, and microvascular dysfunction generate hypoxic tissue environments that can sustain this injurious loop [[228]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32053993). Collectively, these studies suggest that neutrophil degranulation is not merely a marker of inflammation but may also act as an active driver of myocardial injury, extracellular matrix breakdown, ventricular wall thinning, diastolic dysfunction, and impaired cardiac recovery, thereby contributing to the initiation and progression of heart failure.[[223]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35410418) [[224]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35230372) [[225]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30586717) [[226]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34129696) [[227]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33536523) [[228]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32053993) 

Consistent with this literature-based interpretation, the enrichment results provide a quantitative indication that this pathway may be substantially represented in the heart failure-associated protein set. There were 62 heart failure-associated proteins significantly enriched in the pathway of neutrophil degranulation, a quantitatively substantial signal that supports a strong connection between dysregulated innate inflammatory effector activity and heart failure pathobiology. This enrichment indicates that a relatively large protein set converges on a process in which activated neutrophils release granule cargoes, including proteases, oxidant-generating enzymes, antimicrobial peptides, matrix-degrading enzymes, and inflammatory mediators, into phagosomes or the extracellular compartment. From a disease perspective, the size of this enriched protein set, comprising 62 proteins, is consistent with a broad and biologically meaningful involvement of inflammatory tissue injury mechanisms in heart failure, particularly because neutrophil degranulation can simultaneously contribute to clearance of damaged tissue and to collateral injury through oxidative stress, endothelial activation, extracellular matrix degradation, vascular leakage, thrombosis, and amplification of leukocyte recruitment. In ischemic and inflamed cardiac tissue, where hypoxia can further intensify granule release, this pathway has particular relevance to myocardial infarction, ischemia reperfusion injury, ventricular wall thinning, adverse remodeling, and progressive impairment of cardiac function, thereby supporting its interpretation as a double-edged process whose magnitude and timing may critically influence transition toward structural and functional cardiac failure.

To further contextualize this enrichment signal, the network representation below illustrates how the 62 enriched proteins may be interconnected at the protein interaction level.

The figure below shows the protein-protein interaction network for the 62 enriched proteins, and the corresponding STRING webpage is provided for direct network exploration and evidence review.

![PPI Network](imgs/ab035ccd-f6d0-41d0-9149-527c8af6d6f4.png)
![Link to the STRING webpage](https://string-db.org/cgi/link?to=183021E8BEFF15F5)

With this network context in place, the significant proteins identified during the function enrichment analysis can be introduced in a more focused manner. During the function enrichment analysis, we identified serveral significant proteins. We will introduce them in-details in the following.

BST2 is notable in the context of heart failure because inflammatory and antiviral signaling are increasingly recognized as contributors to myocardial injury, adverse remodeling, and progression to heart failure, particularly in viral myocarditis and chronic sterile inflammation. Its established role as an interferon-responsive antiviral effector suggests relevance to cardiotropic viral infections that can precipitate myocarditis and dilated cardiomyopathy. In addition, BST2 can influence nuclear factor kappa B signaling and matrix-remodeling pathways through effects on matrix metallopeptidase fourteen and matrix metallopeptidase fifteen, mechanisms that are directly pertinent to extracellular matrix turnover, fibro-inflammatory remodeling, and ventricular dysfunction. The combined linkage to innate immunity, antiviral defense, inflammatory signaling, and cell migration makes BST2 one of the stronger candidates in this list for a meaningful connection to heart-failure pathobiology.[[174]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18200009) [[175]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18342597) [[176]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19036818) [[177]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19879838) [[178]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/20019814) [[179]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/20399176) [[180]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/20419159) [[181]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/20940320) [[182]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21529378) [[183]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22520941) [[190]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22065321) [[191]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19564354) [[192]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26172439) [[193]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23028328) 

In a related inflammatory framework, CD14 appears highly relevant because it may provide a direct bridge between innate immune sensing and myocardial injury.

CD14 stands out as a highly relevant heart-failure-associated protein because innate immune activation through the CD14 toll like receptor four axis is a well-established driver of systemic and myocardial inflammation. In heart failure, gut barrier dysfunction, endotoxemia, sterile danger signals, and tissue injury can amplify CD14-dependent inflammatory signaling, promoting cytokine production, endothelial activation, adverse ventricular remodeling, and progressive contractile dysfunction. CD14-mediated nuclear factor kappa B activation also aligns with mechanisms implicated in both acute decompensation and chronic heart failure progression. Its role as a central pattern-recognition coreceptor therefore provides a biologically plausible bridge between infection, inflammation, vascular dysfunction, and myocardial remodeling.[[229]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/16148141) [[230]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15895089) [[231]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/8612135) [[232]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19362712) 

Extending from immune activation to the vascular compartment, CD93 may be of interest because endothelial stability and angiogenic capacity are also important determinants of cardiac remodeling.

CD93 is particularly interesting for heart failure because microvascular dysfunction, impaired tissue perfusion, and maladaptive angiogenesis are important determinants of myocardial remodeling and progression to ventricular dysfunction. Proteins that regulate endothelial stability and angiogenic responses may influence the balance between compensatory vascular adaptation and capillary rarefaction in the failing heart. Given its roles in endothelial proliferation, migration, and vessel integrity, CD93 may be relevant to cardiac remodeling, ischemic susceptibility, and the vascular component of heart-failure pathogenesis, especially in settings of pressure overload, ischemic heart disease, or inflammatory vascular injury.[[233]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28435016) [[234]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28671670) [[235]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28912033) 

A complementary perspective is provided by metabolic remodeling, for which FABP5 may represent a plausible link between altered lipid handling and inflammatory signaling.

FABP5 is relevant to heart failure because myocardial energetics and inflammatory lipid signaling are central to disease development. The failing heart undergoes major metabolic reprogramming, including altered fatty-acid handling and nuclear receptor signaling. FABP5 may influence these processes by controlling intracellular lipid trafficking and ligand delivery to transcriptional regulators such as peroxisome proliferator activated receptor delta, which are important for cellular survival and metabolic adaptation. Its additional role in promoting inflammatory prostaglandin synthesis through nuclear factor kappa B further links FABP5 to the chronic low-grade inflammatory state observed in heart failure. Accordingly, FABP5 may connect metabolic dysfunction with inflammatory remodeling, two core features of heart-failure biology.[[236]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12540600) [[237]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/8608126) [[238]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/17512406) [[239]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29531087) [[240]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29440395) 

From metabolic adaptation, the discussion naturally moves to extracellular matrix sensing and fibrotic signaling, where ITGAV appears especially notable.

ITGAV is one of the most compelling heart-failure-related proteins in this list because integrin-mediated mechanotransduction, extracellular matrix sensing, and transforming growth factor beta activation are central mechanisms in cardiac fibrosis and adverse remodeling. Alpha V containing integrins participate in cell-matrix interactions that regulate fibroblast activation, endothelial behavior, wound healing, and tissue stiffness. Of particular importance, ITGAV-containing heterodimers can activate latent transforming growth factor beta one, a master profibrotic cytokine strongly implicated in myocardial fibrosis, ventricular stiffening, and progression to heart failure. Its additional associations with angiogenesis and vascular signaling further strengthen its relevance to structural and functional deterioration of the heart.[[206]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/10025398) [[207]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/9827803) [[208]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25127859) [[209]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/11323698) [[210]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24935931) 

Another potentially relevant layer involves lysosomal and cholesterol homeostasis, which brings NPC2 into consideration.

NPC2 is relevant to heart failure through its role in cellular cholesterol trafficking and lipid homeostasis. Disturbed lipid handling contributes to cardiometabolic disease, lysosomal stress, inflammation, and lipotoxicity, all of which can impair myocardial function. Because lysosomal cholesterol accumulation can alter membrane composition, signaling, mitochondrial function, and inflammatory responses, NPC2 dysfunction or altered regulation may influence cardiomyocyte viability and vascular pathology. Its role in systemic cholesterol handling also suggests potential links to atherosclerotic disease, a major upstream cause of ischemic heart failure.[[241]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12591949) [[242]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/17018531) [[243]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21315718) [[244]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26296895) 

Whereas NPC2 points to intracellular lipid trafficking, OLR1 may connect oxidized lipid recognition more directly to vascular injury and ischemic remodeling.

OLR1 is arguably the strongest cardiovascular candidate in the list. It directly links oxidized lipid uptake to endothelial dysfunction, oxidative stress, inflammation, and atherogenesis, all of which are major antecedents of ischemic heart disease and heart failure. Through nuclear factor kappa B activation, reduced nitric oxide release, and promotion of leukocyte adhesion and apoptosis, OLR1 contributes to vascular injury and impaired perfusion. These mechanisms are highly relevant not only to coronary artery disease leading to heart failure, but also to microvascular dysfunction and systemic vascular inflammation that can worsen cardiac loading conditions and myocardial remodeling. Its additional recognition of advanced glycation end products, apoptotic cells, and bacteria further places OLR1 at the intersection of metabolic stress, inflammation, and vascular pathology.

A somewhat more indirect but still relevant cardiometabolic connection may be considered for PTPRN2.

PTPRN2 is potentially relevant to heart failure primarily through its role in insulin secretion and phosphoinositide-regulated membrane dynamics. Diabetes and insulin resistance are major drivers of heart-failure risk and progression, and proteins that govern insulin vesicle stability and secretion may therefore influence systemic metabolic stress imposed on the myocardium. Beyond endocrine effects, its regulation of phosphatidylinositol four, five bisphosphate and actin dynamics suggests broader relevance to vesicular trafficking and cytoskeletal remodeling, processes that can affect secretory and signaling functions in multiple cell types. Although the connection to heart failure is more indirect than for inflammatory or vascular proteins, PTPRN2 may be important in the cardiometabolic dimension of disease.[[40]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21732083) [[41]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15220191) [[42]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/16418280) [[43]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/16269463) [[44]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19019914) [[45]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12364328) 

Immune sensing remains a recurring theme across this protein set, and RNASET2 adds a potentially important connection to nucleic acid handling and mitochondrial stress responses.

RNASET2 is notable because it connects nucleic-acid sensing, innate immune activation, and mitochondrial ribonucleic acid handling, all of which are increasingly implicated in inflammatory cardiac injury. Toll like receptor seven and toll like receptor eight mediated immune activation can contribute to antiviral responses but may also exacerbate myocardial inflammation during viral infection or sterile tissue damage. In addition, mitochondrial nucleic acid metabolism is highly relevant to cardiomyocyte stress responses, given the centrality of mitochondrial dysfunction in heart failure. Thus, RNASET2 may be mechanistically linked to myocarditis, inflammatory remodeling, and mitochondrial stress signaling in the failing heart.[[245]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31778653) [[246]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38697119) [[247]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28730546) [[248]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30184494) [[249]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30385512) 

Calcium-linked inflammatory signaling offers another possible angle, making S100P a protein of potential interest in this context.

S100P is of interest in heart failure because calcium signaling and receptor for advanced glycation end products mediated inflammatory pathways are both highly relevant to cardiovascular disease. Dysregulated calcium handling is a hallmark of failing cardiomyocytes, while activation of receptor for advanced glycation end products by its ligands contributes to inflammation, fibrosis, oxidative stress, and diabetic cardiovascular complications. Although S100P is less directly established in heart failure than canonical cardiovascular mediators, its ability to engage receptor for advanced glycation end products suggests a plausible role in amplifying inflammatory and profibrotic signaling, particularly in metabolic disease-associated heart failure.

At the level of cellular stress adaptation, TXNDC5 may be relevant because protein folding stress and redox imbalance are frequently implicated in myocardial dysfunction.

TXNDC5 is relevant to heart failure because endoplasmic reticulum stress, oxidative protein folding, and proteostasis failure are important contributors to cardiomyocyte dysfunction and maladaptive remodeling. As a protein disulfide isomerase, TXNDC5 may influence the folding and maturation of secreted and membrane proteins under stress conditions, thereby modulating cellular adaptation to pressure overload, ischemia, or inflammation. Its relation to insulin chemistry further suggests possible links to metabolic disease, which is tightly intertwined with heart-failure pathogenesis. Thus, TXNDC5 may be important at the interface of endoplasmic reticulum stress, redox imbalance, and cardiometabolic dysfunction.[[250]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12930873) [[251]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/14971039) 

Neurohumoral regulation represents an additional dimension of heart failure biology, and ADA2 may be considered within that framework.

ADA2 is relevant to heart failure because chronic sympathetic activation is a defining feature of the syndrome. Alpha two adrenergic signaling modulates catecholamine responses and cyclic adenosine monophosphate generation, processes that influence vascular tone, neurohumoral activation, and cardiac workload. Although this protein is not as directly tied to structural remodeling as some others in the list, altered adrenergic signaling is central to heart-failure progression and therapeutic response. Therefore, ADA2 may contribute to the neurohormonal dysregulation characteristic of heart failure.

Finally, balancing the pro-inflammatory candidates above, LAIR1 may represent a counter-regulatory component within the same broader immune landscape.

LAIR1 is potentially important in heart failure because it represents an endogenous brake on immune activation. Excessive immune-cell activation and cytokine production contribute to chronic inflammation, fibrosis, and ventricular remodeling in heart failure. By suppressing nuclear factor kappa B signaling and inflammatory cytokine output while promoting more tolerogenic immune responses, LAIR1 may counterbalance the inflammatory processes that worsen myocardial injury. This makes it a plausible immunoregulatory factor in inflammatory or autoimmune forms of cardiac dysfunction, even if the connection is more modulatory than primary.

### Pleural mesothelioma (WP:WP5087) 

Pleural mesothelioma is a malignant disease arising from mesothelial cells of the pleura, the serosal membrane surrounding the lungs and lining the thoracic cavity. It is classically associated with prior asbestos exposure and is characterized by long latency, diffuse pleural growth, progressive encasement of the lung, intense local inflammation, stromal remodeling, and marked molecular heterogeneity. Contemporary studies indicate that pleural mesothelioma is not a single biologic entity but rather a spectrum of tumors defined by differences in morphology, genomic instability, immune response, methylation state, and recurrent alterations involving genes such as BRCA1 associated protein 1, neurofibromin 2, and cyclin dependent kinase inhibitor 2A. Therapeutically, management includes surgery in highly selected patients, platinum and pemetrexed based chemotherapy, immune checkpoint blockade, antiangiogenic therapy, and emerging biomarker guided approaches. Recent randomized and phase two studies have shown clinically meaningful activity for nivolumab plus ipilimumab in unresectable disease, durvalumab combined with platinum and pemetrexed, ramucirumab plus gemcitabine in previously treated disease, pegargiminase with first line chemotherapy in nonepithelioid tumors, and enhancer of zeste homolog 2 inhibition in biomarker selected relapsed disease. At the same time, multimodality local therapy can impose substantial cardiopulmonary stress, and randomized surgical evidence suggests increased serious cardiac and respiratory toxicity with aggressive pleural surgery. Thus, although pleural mesothelioma is primarily a thoracic malignancy rather than a canonical heart failure signaling pathway, it intersects with heart failure through shared inflammatory and vascular biology, direct cardiopulmonary mechanical burden, and treatment related cardiovascular toxicity.  

Building on this clinical and biologic context, the relationship between pleural mesothelioma and heart failure appears to be chiefly clinical and pathobiological rather than a direct causal heart failure pathway. First, pleural mesothelioma develops within the thoracic cavity and produces progressive pleural thickening, restrictive lung mechanics, hypoxemia, pulmonary vascular stress, recurrent pleural effusions, and chronic systemic inflammation; together, these processes may increase right ventricular afterload, worsen pre existing cardiac dysfunction, and precipitate decompensation in susceptible patients. Second, several treatments used in pleural mesothelioma have documented cardiovascular consequences that are directly relevant to heart failure. In the phase three trial of nivolumab plus ipilimumab for unresectable malignant pleural mesothelioma, treatment related death from heart failure was reported, demonstrating that immune checkpoint therapy can rarely trigger severe cardiovascular toxicity in this population [[252]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33485464). In the randomized trial comparing extended pleurectomy decortication plus chemotherapy with chemotherapy alone, the surgical strategy produced substantially more serious adverse events, including a higher incidence of cardiac disorders, indicating that aggressive resection can impose major hemodynamic and cardiopulmonary stress that may contribute to heart failure risk [[253]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38740044). The surgery after radiotherapy protocol also showed frequent severe perioperative morbidity after hemithoracic radiotherapy followed by extrapleural pneumonectomy, further supporting the concept that intensive local therapy can challenge cardiovascular reserve [[254]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33450184). Antiangiogenic treatment provides another mechanistic link: ramucirumab improved survival in pretreated pleural mesothelioma but increased severe hypertension and thromboembolic toxicity, both established contributors to cardiac dysfunction and heart failure progression [[255]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34499874). More broadly, multiomic studies show that pleural mesothelioma is shaped by immune activation, stromal remodeling, and interpatient biologic heterogeneity, while spatial profiling demonstrates marked variation in extracellular matrix pathways and immune mediator expression across tumor sites; these features are relevant because inflammatory cytokine signaling, fibrosis, and vascular remodeling are central drivers of adverse cardiac remodeling in heart failure, suggesting overlapping disease biology even if the primary disease is malignant rather than cardiac [[256]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36928603) [[257]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34261524). Therefore, pleural mesothelioma is related to heart failure through thoracic mechanical burden, inflammation associated cardiopulmonary compromise, and especially through treatment associated cardiac toxicity, making cardiovascular assessment and surveillance important in affected patients.[[252]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33485464) [[253]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38740044) [[254]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33450184) [[255]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34499874) [[256]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36928603) [[257]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34261524) 

With this disease level connection established, the enrichment results provide a molecular framework that may help contextualize the overlap between pleural mesothelioma biology and heart failure associated processes. There were 46 heart failure-associated proteins significantly enriched in the pathway describing pleural mesothelioma as a malignant disease of pleural mesothelial cells characterized by asbestos associated pathogenesis, prolonged latency, diffuse pleural growth, stromal remodeling, inflammatory activation, molecular heterogeneity, and clinically important interactions with cardiopulmonary stress and cardiovascular toxicity. This enrichment set contains a substantial number of proteins, with a total count of 46, supporting a biologically meaningful overlap between heart failure related molecular features and the inflammatory, vascular, remodeling, and treatment associated processes represented in pleural mesothelioma.

To further illustrate this overlap at the network level, the figure below presents the protein-protein interaction network for these 46 proteins, and the corresponding STRING webpage can be accessed through the embedded link for further network level inspection.

![PPI Network](imgs/118bf332-4515-48c9-9db0-131440d8f979.png)
![Link to the STRING webpage](https://string-db.org/cgi/link?to=785EB4A4B9CBBE22)

Following this network overview, the function enrichment analysis highlighted several proteins that may be particularly informative for interpreting the possible relationship to heart failure. During the function enrichment analysis, we identified serveral significant proteins. We will introduce them in-details in the following.

Among the listed proteins, MDK stands out as one of the most directly relevant to heart failure because it links several core pathogenic processes, including inflammation, vascular remodeling, tissue repair, and cell survival. The supplied functional annotation indicates that MDK recruits neutrophils and macrophages to sites of injury, modulates dendritic cell and T-cell responses, and promotes survival signaling via MAPK and AKT pathways. Importantly, it is specifically noted to participate in tissue regeneration after heart damage by negatively regulating inflammatory cell recruitment and supporting cell survival through anti-apoptotic and angiogenic mechanisms. These properties are highly pertinent to heart failure, in which maladaptive inflammation, cardiomyocyte loss, microvascular insufficiency, and fibrotic remodeling collectively drive ventricular dysfunction. MDK also promotes smooth muscle cell migration and VEGFA-related endothelial responses, suggesting a role in vascular remodeling that may influence myocardial perfusion and afterload. In addition, its ability to induce epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition and regulate repair-associated cell plasticity suggests possible relevance to adverse remodeling and fibrosis. Taken together, MDK appears to be a multifunctional stress-response mediator with plausible roles in both compensatory repair and maladaptive remodeling in failing hearts.[[129]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/10212223) [[137]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/10683378) [[130]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/10772929) [[131]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12084985) [[132]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12122009) [[133]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12573468) [[134]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15466886) [[135]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18469519) [[138]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22323540) [[136]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24458438) 

Closely related to this vascular and repair oriented theme, VEGFA is highly relevant to heart failure because impaired angiogenesis, endothelial dysfunction, altered vascular permeability, and defective nitric oxide bioavailability are major contributors to myocardial ischemia, adverse remodeling, and progressive pump failure. The annotation describes VEGFA as an essential mediator of endothelial proliferation, migration, survival, and differentiation, while also promoting NOS2 and NOS3 activation and nitric oxide production. These functions are central to maintaining coronary microvascular integrity and myocardial perfusion. In the failing heart, insufficient vascular adaptation relative to hypertrophic growth can exacerbate hypoxia and fibrosis, whereas dysregulated VEGFA signaling may also contribute to edema and pathological vascular permeability. The described activation of AKT, ERK, PI3K, SRC, and FAK further places VEGFA at the center of survival and remodeling pathways relevant to both endothelial and potentially cardiac stromal responses. Therefore, VEGFA-related signaling is mechanistically connected to the vascular and microcirculatory dimensions of heart failure pathogenesis.

Extending from vascular signaling to structural remodeling, ACTA2 is relevant to heart failure primarily because it is a canonical smooth muscle and myofibroblast-associated cytoskeletal protein, and the provided function emphasizes its role in motility and actin-based cellular structure. In the context of heart failure, actin remodeling is fundamental to vascular tone regulation, fibroblast-to-myofibroblast transition, and extracellular matrix remodeling. Increased ACTA2 expression is often interpreted as a marker of activated myofibroblasts and vascular smooth muscle remodeling, both of which contribute to myocardial stiffening, fibrosis, and altered hemodynamics. Although the supplied annotation is general, its implication for contractile and migratory cellular phenotypes makes ACTA2 particularly relevant to adverse cardiac remodeling, especially in pressure overload, hypertensive heart disease, and fibrotic progression.

In a similar extracellular matrix context, CTHRC1 is potentially important in heart failure because collagen accumulation and extracellular matrix expansion are central determinants of myocardial fibrosis, ventricular stiffening, and impaired diastolic and systolic performance. A protein that negatively regulates collagen matrix deposition may influence whether tissue repair remains adaptive or progresses toward pathological fibrosis. In heart failure, excessive collagen deposition increases chamber stiffness, disrupts electrical and mechanical coupling, and worsens remodeling. Therefore, CTHRC1 may represent a matrix-modifying factor with possible antifibrotic significance. Even though the supplied annotation is concise, its direct connection to collagen regulation makes it biologically relevant to fibrotic mechanisms that underlie many forms of heart failure, particularly heart failure with preserved ejection fraction and post-injury remodeling.

Moving from matrix regulation to developmental and inflammatory signaling, ROR1 is of interest in heart failure because non-canonical WNT signaling, inflammatory NFkB activation, and receptor-mediated remodeling pathways are increasingly implicated in cardiac fibrosis, hypertrophy, and ventricular remodeling. The provided annotation identifies ROR1 as a receptor for WNT5A, a ligand frequently associated with inflammatory and profibrotic signaling rather than developmental canonical WNT responses. Through NFkB activation and possible antagonism of WNT3A-mediated signaling, ROR1 could influence fibroblast activation, inflammatory crosstalk, and maladaptive tissue remodeling. Although the evidence here is less directly cardiac than for MDK or VEGFA, the WNT5A-ROR1 axis is mechanistically plausible in heart failure because inflammatory signaling and altered developmental pathways often re-emerge in injured myocardium and contribute to structural deterioration.[[258]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25029443) [[259]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27162350) [[260]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36949068) 

Shifting to the metabolic dimension of heart failure, FABP4 is relevant through its connection to systemic metabolic dysfunction, lipid handling, and adipose-cardiovascular crosstalk. The supplied annotation emphasizes its role in long-chain fatty acid and retinoic acid transport to nuclear receptors, indicating a function in lipid signaling and transcriptional regulation. Since metabolic syndrome, insulin resistance, obesity, and lipotoxicity are major drivers of heart failure risk and progression, FABP4 may be particularly important in cardiometabolic forms of disease. Elevated adipocyte-derived lipid signaling can contribute indirectly to endothelial dysfunction, inflammation, and altered myocardial substrate utilization. Thus, although FABP4 is not a classical structural heart failure gene, its biology is highly relevant to the metabolic environment that predisposes to and aggravates heart failure.

Finally, in comparison with the more directly vascular, inflammatory, and matrix associated proteins above, MAD1L1 appears to have a more indirect connection to heart failure. MAD1L1 is less directly connected to heart failure than the vascular, inflammatory, and matrix-remodeling proteins in this list, but it may still be relevant in the context of proliferating non-myocyte populations such as fibroblasts, endothelial cells, and immune cells. The annotation shows that MAD1L1 is essential for mitotic checkpoint control and genomic stability. In heart failure, pathological remodeling depends in part on expansion and activation of stromal and vascular cell populations, and dysregulated cell-cycle control in these compartments could influence fibrosis, vascular rarefaction, or reparative responses after injury. Nevertheless, compared with MDK, VEGFA, ACTA2, and CTHRC1, the connection of MAD1L1 to heart failure is more indirect and likely reflects general proliferative biology rather than a specific established mechanism of cardiac dysfunction.[[261]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/10700282) [[262]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/11804586) [[263]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15024386) [[264]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29162720)

### Extracellular matrix organization (REAC:R-HSA-1474244) 

Extracellular matrix organization is the coordinated process by which structural proteins, adhesive glycoproteins, proteoglycans, matrix-modifying enzymes, and matricellular regulators are synthesized, assembled, cross-linked, aligned, remodeled, and degraded to generate a functional tissue scaffold. This pathway influences not only tissue architecture and mechanical strength, but also cell adhesion, migration, differentiation, survival, and signal transduction, because the extracellular matrix serves as both a biomechanical framework and a reservoir for growth factors and cytokines. The publications provided collectively highlight several central features of this pathway. During cardiac development, proper extracellular matrix organization is required for epicardial progenitor migration and morphogenesis of the atrial ventricular canal, suggesting that cardiac cells depend on tightly regulated matrix composition and spatial patterning for normal heart formation [[265]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30650362). Mechanical cues also appear to be major determinants of extracellular matrix organization, as force-dependent transforming growth factor beta signaling regulates matrix production and cellular morphology in connective tissues [[266]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30475205). In ageing cardiac tissue, extracellular matrix remodeling involves both biochemical composition and tissue stiffness, and these matrix properties directly influence cardiac fibroblast activation, senescence, and profibrotic behavior [[267]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40506498). Additional studies indicate that extracellular matrix organization is shaped by pathways involving integrins, matrix metallopeptidases, collagen cross-linking enzymes, and adhesion regulators, all of which influence how cells sense and respond to their microenvironment [[268]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32649911) [[269]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38472175) [[270]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40211949). Taken together, this pathway may be viewed as a dynamic and tightly regulated program that integrates structural remodeling, mechanotransduction, and cell signaling, and is therefore likely to be important for tissue homeostasis, repair, ageing, and chronic disease.

Against this broader biological background, the potential relevance of extracellular matrix organization to heart failure becomes more coherent. Extracellular matrix organization is highly relevant to heart failure because heart failure is fundamentally a disease of maladaptive cardiac remodeling in which changes in matrix composition, stiffness, alignment, turnover, and cell-matrix signaling progressively impair ventricular structure and function. The most directly informative study among the provided publications shows that in ageing cardiac tissue, extracellular matrix remodeling alters both ligand presentation and mechanical stiffness, and that these two features independently regulate cardiac fibroblast activation, matrix remodeling, and senescence; importantly, a youthful extracellular matrix composition can suppress profibrotic fibroblast behavior even in a stiff environment, demonstrating that matrix organization is not merely a passive consequence of disease but may also act as an active determinant of cardiac cellular state [[267]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40506498). This observation is highly pertinent to heart failure, where activated cardiac fibroblasts drive interstitial and perivascular fibrosis, increase ventricular stiffness, and disrupt electromechanical coupling. Developmental evidence further supports the cardiac importance of this pathway, as ten-eleven translocation enzyme dependent regulation of extracellular matrix organization is required for epicardial progenitor migration and heart morphogenesis in zebrafish, indicating that the heart is intrinsically dependent on precise matrix patterning for normal tissue assembly and implying that later-life matrix disorganization may also have major functional consequences [[265]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30650362). Mechanistic studies in other systems reinforce concepts that may be transferable to heart failure pathobiology: mechanical force can induce transforming growth factor beta dependent extracellular matrix production and cellular remodeling [[266]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30475205), integrin-mediated matrix assembly controls downstream signaling environments [[268]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32649911), hypoxia-inducible factor one alpha signaling can couple metabolism to collagen organization and cross-linking through procollagen lysine hydroxylation and lysyl oxidase pathways [[269]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38472175), and impaired endothelial adhesion with defective matrix organization can itself drive cardiopulmonary vascular disease that is reversible with matrix metallopeptidase inhibition [[270]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40211949). Taken together, these studies support a model in which disturbed extracellular matrix organization may contribute to heart failure by promoting fibroblast activation, collagen deposition and cross-linking, excessive tissue stiffening, abnormal force transmission, endothelial dysfunction, and persistent profibrotic signaling, thereby accelerating adverse cardiac remodeling and functional decline.[[265]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30650362) [[266]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30475205) [[267]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40506498) [[268]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32649911) [[269]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38472175) [[270]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40211949) 

This conceptual framework is further supported by the enrichment results obtained in the present analysis. There were 62 heart failure-associated proteins significantly enriched in the pathway of extracellular matrix organization, indicating a substantial convergence of disease-related molecular signals on the regulation of tissue scaffold assembly, remodeling, and degradation. This enrichment is highly consistent with the central role of extracellular matrix dynamics in cardiac structure and function, because extracellular matrix organization governs mechanical strength, cell adhesion, migration, differentiation, survival, and signal transduction through the coordinated control of structural proteins, adhesive glycoproteins, proteoglycans, matrix-modifying enzymes, and matricellular regulators. The biological relevance of this pathway to the heart is strongly supported by evidence showing that proper extracellular matrix organization is required for epicardial progenitor migration and morphogenesis of the atrial ventricular canal during cardiac development [[265]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30650362). In parallel, force-dependent transforming growth factor beta signaling has been shown to regulate matrix production and cellular morphology, demonstrating that biomechanical stress is quantitatively and functionally integrated into extracellular matrix remodeling programs [[266]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30475205). In ageing cardiac tissue, extracellular matrix remodeling is further linked to altered biochemical composition and increased stiffness, both of which directly influence cardiac fibroblast activation, senescence, and profibrotic behavior, thereby providing a mechanistic bridge between age-related matrix alterations and progressive cardiac dysfunction [[267]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40506498). Additional studies indicate that this pathway is shaped by integrin signaling, matrix metallopeptidase activity, collagen cross-linking enzymes, and adhesion regulators, together forming a multicomponent network that controls how cardiac cells sense and respond to their surrounding microenvironment [[268]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32649911) [[269]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38472175) [[270]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40211949). Taken together, the identification of 62 enriched proteins supports the interpretation that extracellular matrix organization is not a peripheral process in heart failure, but rather a quantitatively prominent and biologically integrated pathway that links structural remodeling, mechanotransduction, ageing-associated stiffness, and maladaptive repair.

To complement this enrichment-based interpretation, the interaction structure of these 62 proteins is shown below. Figure below illustrates the protein-protein interaction network of these 62 proteins, and the corresponding STRING webpage is provided for interactive network exploration.

![PPI Network](imgs/7e685679-0e3c-4e3b-a25c-200332af7d84.png)
![Link to the STRING webpage](https://string-db.org/cgi/link?to=14D6FDE86EB0D8D0)

Building on the pathway-level view, the following section introduces several significant proteins identified during the function enrichment analysis. During the function enrichment analysis, we identified serveral significant proteins. We will introduce them in-details in the following.

Among the proteins listed, BMP10 stands out as the most directly relevant to heart failure because its annotated function is intrinsically linked to cardiac development and vascular signaling. Its requirement for embryonic cardiomyocyte proliferation, together with maintenance of MEF2C and NKX2-5 expression, indicates a central role in establishing and preserving cardiac muscle cell programs. These developmental pathways are highly pertinent to heart failure because many forms of cardiac remodeling recapitulate fetal or developmental signaling networks, and perturbation of cardiomyocyte growth control can influence myocardial structure, contractile reserve, and susceptibility to decompensation. Moreover, BMP10 signaling through ALK receptors and SMAD1/5/8 suggests involvement in endothelial-cardiac crosstalk, which is relevant to vascular homeostasis, pulmonary vascular remodeling, and cardiac loading conditions that contribute to heart failure progression. Its inhibitory effects on endothelial migration and growth further imply a role in vascular remodeling, a process that can influence myocardial perfusion and maladaptive remodeling. Although the provided annotation does not directly describe adult heart failure, BMP10 appears to be the strongest candidate for meaningful mechanistic relevance because it connects cardiomyocyte biology, developmental cardiac transcriptional control, and endothelial signaling.

With this cardiac-developmental context in mind, the next proteins may be considered more indirectly connected, primarily through extracellular matrix remodeling, inflammation, and vascular biology. ADAM9 is of potential interest in heart failure primarily because its substrates and associated processes converge on vascular remodeling, endothelial signaling, inflammation, and extracellular matrix interactions, all of which are central components of heart failure pathophysiology. Cleavage of angiogenesis-related receptors and adhesion molecules such as TEK, KDR, VCAM1, and CDH5 suggests that ADAM9 could modulate endothelial integrity, leukocyte-endothelial communication, and neovascular responses. In heart failure, especially in ischemic or inflammatory settings, these processes influence myocardial perfusion, capillary rarefaction, endothelial dysfunction, and adverse remodeling. Its reported capacity to regulate cell motility via integrins further supports a role in matrix-dependent remodeling, which is highly relevant to fibrosis and structural progression of failing myocardium. While the annotation is not heart-specific, ADAM9 stands out because it intersects with several biological mechanisms that are repeatedly implicated in heart failure progression, particularly angiogenesis and inflammatory vascular remodeling.[[171]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19273593) [[172]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/9920899) [[173]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/10825303) 

A related line of reasoning extends to proteins involved in immune-cell recruitment. ADAM8 is potentially relevant to heart failure because leukocyte extravasation is a key step in inflammatory cell recruitment to injured or stressed tissues, including the myocardium. Inflammatory infiltration contributes to cardiac remodeling, fibrosis, and progressive functional decline in multiple forms of heart failure, including post-ischemic, pressure-overload, and myocarditis-associated disease. Therefore, a protein implicated in leukocyte trafficking may influence the intensity or persistence of myocardial inflammation. Although the provided annotation is brief and does not establish a direct cardiac role, ADAM8 is notable because immune-cell recruitment is increasingly recognized as an important determinant of adverse remodeling and heart failure progression.

Finally, ICAM5 may be considered within the same broader inflammatory framework, although the evidence presented here appears more indirect. ICAM5 has a plausible but comparatively indirect relationship to heart failure through its role in leukocyte adhesion. Adhesion between leukocytes and endothelial or tissue ligands is a prerequisite for inflammatory cell recruitment, and immune activation is a well-established contributor to cardiac remodeling and dysfunction. Because LFA-1-mediated adhesive interactions participate in leukocyte retention and activation, proteins that engage this pathway can, in principle, modulate inflammatory burden. However, based on the information provided, ICAM5 is less compelling than BMP10, ADAM9, or ADAM8 because its annotation does not indicate a specific role in cardiac tissue, vascular remodeling, or myocardial signaling. Its relevance is therefore mechanistically conceivable but more tentative.
